topic: Web Browsers, Search Engines, and Email
description: An exam-oriented overview covering the fundamental tools required to navigate the internet. It details the functionalities, history, and protocols associated with web browsers, search engines, and electronic mail.

sections.title: Web Browsers
sections.description: Software applications utilized to access, retrieve, and navigate content on the World Wide Web.

key_concepts.explanation: A client-side software application used to access information on the World Wide Web (WWW). It requests data from web servers and displays the resulting web pages.
The unique global address of a web page or resource on the internet, which is typed into the browser's address bar to access that specific page.

historical_events.event: Creation of the First Web Browser
historical_events.significance: Tim Berners-Lee invented the first web browser named 'WorldWideWeb', which was later renamed to 'Nexus' to avoid confusion with the WWW space itself.
Developed by Marc Andreessen, Mosaic is widely credited as the first popular graphical web browser that helped popularize the internet.

key_associations.extra_info: Currently the world's most widely used web browser, built on the open-source Chromium project and utilizing the Blink rendering engine.
Launched initially as the default browser for Windows 10, officially replacing the legacy Internet Explorer.
The default, proprietary web browser integrated into all iOS and macOS devices.

sections.title: Search Engines
sections.description: Information retrieval systems designed to search for and index information on the World Wide Web.

key_concepts.explanation: A software system designed to carry out web searches. It looks through its database to find items corresponding to the keywords entered by the user and displays them on a Search Engine Results Page (SERP).
An automated script or internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web for the purpose of web indexing (updating the search engine's database).

key_associations.extra_info: Developed in 1998, it dominates the global market share and is the most utilized search engine in the world.
Microsoft's official search engine, which replaced Live Search, and serves as the primary competitor to Google.
A search engine famous for protecting searchers' privacy by avoiding personalized search results and completely refusing to track user search queries.

important_facts.fact: 'Archie' is widely acknowledged as the world's first search engine, created in 1990 by Alan Emtage to search FTP archives.

sections.title: Electronic Mail (Email)
sections.description: The digital message exchange system and the vital network protocols that govern its operation.

key_concepts.explanation: An electronic method of composing, sending, storing, and receiving digital messages over electronic communication systems like the internet.
CC (Carbon Copy) makes the copied email addresses visible to all other recipients. BCC (Blind Carbon Copy) keeps the copied recipients' identities hidden from one another.

historical_events.significance: Sent by computer engineer Ray Tomlinson. He is also credited with introducing the '@' symbol to logically separate the username from the destination server's name.

key_associations.extra_info: The industry-standard protocol used for transmitting outbound emails across the internet from a client to a server (typically utilizes Port 25).
Used by local email clients to retrieve emails from a remote server, usually deleting the messages from the server once downloaded.
Allows users to read and manage emails directly on the server without deleting them, making it ideal for syncing mail across multiple devices seamlessly.

sections.title: Important Terminology and Concepts
sections.description: Crucial technical vocabulary associated with web browsing and internet data management.

key_concepts.explanation: Small blocks of text data saved on a user's computer by a web browser while the user is browsing. They are used to remember stateful information like login details and site preferences.
A temporary storage location on the local hard drive where web browsers store copies of frequently accessed web pages, images, and scripts to drastically improve load times upon subsequent visits.
A browser feature that allows users to permanently save the URL of a specific web page to easily and directly navigate back to it in the future.

important_facts.fact: 'Spam' is the term used to describe unsolicited, unwanted, or junk emails that are sent out in bulk to a massive list of recipients, often for advertising or malicious purposes.
Standard HTTP uses Port 80 for unencrypted web traffic, whereas HTTPS uses Port 443 to secure communication over a computer network via TLS/SSL encryption.

sections.title: Major Browser Shortcut Keys
sections.description: Common keyboard shortcuts utilized to expedite navigation and operations on modern web browsers.

key_associations.extra_info: Opens a new, blank tab directly within the active browser window.
Opens the history panel or tab, displaying the chronological list of all previously visited web pages.
Opens the browser's downloads interface to view the status and list of all downloaded files.
Opens a new private browsing window in Google Chrome where local data like history, form inputs, and cookies are not saved after closing.
Forces the browser to reload the currently active web page to fetch the most recent data.
